Spearman rho=-0.0639, p=0.099717, n=665 (no clear full-rank signal). Kruskal-Wallis H=32.9723, p=2.7e-05. Mann-Whitney BEST 1.257 (n=56) vs AVOID 1.092 (n=160), U=5546.0, p=0.004018. Trigger accuracy rho=0.4525, n=121.

A R2=0.763 OOS 0.761; C R2=0.902 OOS 0.919; dR2=+0.139. Offensive-control components add +0.005 R2 beyond ORtg. Net~ORtg+leakage R2=0.948. corr(leakage, DRtg)=+0.894. PCI univariate r=+0.863 vs ORtg +0.866.

[APPM-017] C gamma +0.0714 SE 0.0057 p=0.0000; B DiD +0.062 [0.051,0.073]; proxy agrees with production engine 13/79 = 16.5%. [CHT-024] A +0.047 PPP (p<10^-3); B +0.062 PPP; C +0.0714 PPP, n=16,921 cells, p<10^-4. Coverage: 9,853 RS pairs; 35.7% clear, 33.8% ambiguous, 30.4% no_rec.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Hit rate test of engine top recommendation versus team modal play type
failed_approaches.why: Artifact produced by lookahead leakage and labeling flaw; small sample limited power (n=53)

failed_approaches.what_failed: Ranked playsheet validation of recommended counter rankings
failed_approaches.why: Inconclusive due to small sample, lookahead leakage, and low measurement reliability

failed_approaches.what_failed: Incremental R² test of Possession Control Index over ORtg
failed_approaches.why: Artifact from mechanical floor: PCI was a proxy for DRtg, and leakage inflated apparent explanatory power

failed_approaches.what_failed: Possession-level test of proxy matchup-conditioned play-type picker
failed_approaches.why: Inconclusive because proxy fidelity was low (16.5%), in-sample contamination leaked signals, and i.i.d. standard errors were used

evidence_establishes: The engine's play-type recommendations have exhibited fragile signal in small-sample studies, often contaminated by lookahead leakage
No prior study has directly tested whether adhering to a recommended mix predicts winning
Multiple earlier validation studies were flagged as artifact or inconclusive
evidence_does_not_establish: That adherence to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts series or game outcomes
That the engine's recommended mix is causally effective or even directionally correct outside of curated settings
That a test of the question is impossible; rather it shows that careful design is required to avoid known pitfalls
own_inferences: The recommendation engine's quality is not yet validated, so a test of adherence mixes the engine's validity with adherence behaviour; the question is testable as a joint hypothesis but risks being uninterpretable if the engine is poor
Using per-game adherence instead of per-series adherence would increase sample size from 54 to approximately 300 games, improving power
Strict temporal separation is the only way to avoid lookahead leakage: the recommended mix must be defined using data that was available before the game in which adherence is measured
uncertainties: Whether a stable suppression-conditional recommended mix can be estimated from regular season data, given that defensive strategies and personnel change
The reliability of play-type classification and suppression detection in the derived possession data
The extent to which adherence to a recommended mix is confounded by general team quality, injuries, or strategic adjustments outside the scope of the engine

historical_effect.explanation: Without the historical record, a naive series-level correlation might have been attempted, risking lookahead artifacts and low power. The evidence of lookahead-induced artifacts in similar studies (SF-APPS-003, SF-APPS-068) and inconclusive small-sample results (SF-APPS-018) directly motivates a design that uses per-game analysis, out-of-sample recommendation generation, and pre-registered falsification.

blocking_constraints.text: Using any data from the same series (or future games) to define recommended mix would inflate apparent effect and produce an artifact
54 series with a binary outcome is underpowered; shifting to per-game analysis mitigates but does not eliminate power concerns
Defense suppression profiles and recommended mix rely on accurate play-type tagging and matchup assignments, which may be noisy

prior_work.summary: No earlier study addressed whether adhering to a recommended mix predicts winning; previous work evaluated recommendation hit rates (artifact, inconclusive) and the statistical properties of the engine's components.

risks.text: Defining the recommended mix using data from the same series or later games would create an apparent predictive relationship that is not real
A series-level binary-outcome test with 54 units has low power for realistic effect sizes; a per-game design with series-level clustering is needed
The defense's suppression tendencies and the engine's recommended mix depend on play-type labels that may be inconsistently applied or sparsely observed
Adherence could be correlated with opponent defensive weakness, general team offensive skill, or strategic adjustments that are not captured by the engine's suppression model
Defensive strategies evolve across seasons and even within a playoff series, so a static suppression profile may misrepresent the true defensive context

design.estimand: The effect of per-game adherence to the suppression-conditional recommended offensive mix on game win probability, conditional on opponent and context.
design.sample: All playoff games from 2022-23 through 2025-26 for which a defense suppression profile and recommended mix can be estimated using only data prior to that series (e.g., regular season of the same year and earlier playoff rounds), with exact dates fixed before analysis.
design.power: Approximately 300 games; logistic mixed-effects model with series-level random intercepts. A detectable increase in win probability of at least 5 percentage points per standard deviation increase in adherence at 80% power is plausible; exact power will be assessed via simulation prior to unblinding.
design.controls: Team offensive rating (prior regular season), opponent defensive rating, home/away indicator, days of rest, and a binary indicator for key injuries (from a pre-registered source).
design.falsification: 1) Permute the recommended play-type list within each game and test whether adherence to a random list predicts outcome; 2) replace adherence with a metric of general offensive efficiency not conditional on suppression to ensure the effect is incremental to overall quality.
design.multiplicity: Single pre-registered adherence metric: proportion of offensive half-court possessions using a play type ranked in the top 3 of the recommended counter list, with possessions weighted equally.
design.decision_rule: One-sided test that the adherence coefficient is positive at α=0.025 (after a planned Bonferroni correction for any secondary metrics). The result will be interpreted only if the falsification checks do not suggest artifact.
design.data_version: Play-by-play and possession data snapshots as of 2026-06-16, using point-in-time logic to exclude information unavailable before each game. The exact code generating recommended mixes will be frozen before any predictive test.

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.

The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["defensive suppression", "recommended defensive mix", "adherence to recommended strategy", "winning"], "methodological_questions": ["measurement of recommended mix", "adherence metric", "outcome definition", "confounding by opponent strength", "sample size series level"], "query": "adhering to recommended defensive mix predicts winning"}}

reasoning_details.text:
We need to perform stage 1: retrieval. The research question: "Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning." Need to identify research concepts and methodological questions. Let's break it down.

Research concepts: 
- Defensive suppression
- Counter strategy (best/avoid)
- "recommended mix" suggests a mixture of defensive strategies, perhaps a blend of actions? Might be related to defensive play-calling, mixing coverage types, etc.
- "adherence" to that mix
- Predicting winning (team success)

Methodological questions: 
- How to define "suppression-conditional recommended mix"? Probably derived from some model that recommends a defensive mix conditioned on opponent's offensive tendencies? 
- How to measure adherence? (maybe distance from recommended distribution of defensive actions)
- Outcome: winning (game, series, season? The units are 54 series, so maybe series-level)
- Data: per-game, play-by-play, defensive matchup minutes, play-type possession records. 
- Need to consider potential confounders, sample size (54 series), measurement reliability, etc.

Query should capture: suppression, recommended mix, adherence, winning.

Let's craft the retrieval call. Use retrieve_history with the required args. I'll specify research_concepts and methodological_questions as arrays of strings, and a query string combining them.

Make sure to follow the protocol: only one JSON object, action "tool", tool "retrieve_history", args with those fields. No extra text.

Let's propose:
research_concepts: ["defensive suppression", "recommended defensive mix", "adherence to recommended strategy", "winning"]
methodological_questions: ["measurement of recommended mix", "adherence metric", "outcome definition", "confounding by opponent strength", "sample size series level"]
query: "adhering to recommended defensive mix predicts winning"

I'll output that.

We need to process stage 2 with the retrieval results. We have four families: FAM:SF-APPS-003, FAM:SF-APPS-018, FAM:SF-APPS-068, FAM:SF37. We need to summarize historical evidence, failed approaches, assess testability, etc. The research question: "Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning." Area: defensive suppression and counter strategy. We need to decide whether to proceed.

First, understand the question. "Suppression-conditional recommended mix" likely refers to a defensive scheme that involves suppressing certain offensive plays, and then recommends a mix of counters (play types) to use on offense based on the defense's suppression. The hypothesis is that if a team adheres to that recommended mix (i.e., follows the recommendations), it predicts winning (presumably at the series level, given 54 series). Data: per-game NBA stats for 2022-23 to 2025-26 seasons, with play-by-play, defensive matchups, derived play-type possession records. Units: 54 series (playoff series? The data says regular season and playoffs, but units are 54 series; probably playoff series across those seasons. 2022-23 playoffs (16 teams, 15 series? Actually 8 first round, 4 conf semis, 2 conf finals, 1 finals = 15 series per year, so 4 years = 60 series, but some may not be fully available? 2025-26 playoffs only complete from 2026-06-21, but research question date is 2026-06-16, so maybe partial? Units available: 54 series. So likely all completed series from 2022-23 to 2025-26? 2022-23 playoffs: 15 series; 2023-24: 15; 2024-25: 15; 2025-26: maybe only 9 series completed by June 16? That sums to 54. So all series from those years.

The question is about "adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning." So we need to define: for each possession, the defense's suppression strategy (what play types they are suppressing), the recommended mix of offensive play types to counter that suppression, and then a metric of adherence (how closely the offense followed that recommended mix). Then aggregate to series level and see if higher adherence correlates with winning the series.

Relevant retrieved families:
- FAM:SF-APPS-003: SQ2 decision quality hit rate: engine top pt_shift vs team modal PT. This compares the engine's recommended play type to team's highest-volume play type in playoff series. Outcome status: artifact. They found 69.8% hit rate but artifact due to leakage lookahead and small sample. So this is about recommended vs actual play, not directly about adherence to a mix predicting winning, but relevant: it shows that the engine's recommendation outperforms modal? But artifact. So the engine's recommendation quality may be flawed.
- FAM:SF-APPS-018: Ranked playsheet validation, 10 series. Tests whether playsheet counter ranking predicts which alternative scored better when defense drops a play type >=0.25 PPP H1 to H2. Inconclusive, with risks: drift, leakage, measurement reliability, small sample. They found some signal (Mann-Whitney BEST > AVOID), but full ranking not clear. This involves recommended mix (BEST>AVOID) and scoring outcomes. Not directly "adherence predicts winning" but rather recommendation quality.
- FAM:SF-APPS-068: Possession Control Index incremental R2 over ORtg. Artifact because PCI is a DRtg proxy, basically leakage. Not directly relevant to suppression-conditional mix adherence.
- FAM:SF37: Possession-level SQ2 test: proxy engine on all RS games. Inconclusive, small sample, leakage. Tests whether matchup-conditioned PT picker has signal. Not directly adherence to mix.

So none of the retrieved studies directly tested "adherence to recommended mix predicts winning." They tested engine recommendation quality (which play type is best), not whether following the engine's recommendations leads to winning. However, they show risks and failures: lookahead leakage (using future outcomes to define recommendations?), measurement reliability, small sample, artifact risk from constructing labels based on performance. So these are relevant as historical evidence of failed approaches and methodological pitfalls.

We need to assess whether this research question is testable with the data. The data include play-by-play, defensive matchups, derived play-type possession records, etc. So we can construct for each series: the defensive suppression patterns (how the defense adjusts its coverage of play types), the recommended mix (which play types should be used to counter that defense), and the actual offensive play-type mix. Then adherence could be measured as similarity (e.g., proportion of possessions where the offense used a recommended play type, or correlation between recommended frequency and actual frequency). Winning is binary outcome (win series or not). But 54 series is a small sample for binary outcome with a continuous adherence metric; power would be low. Also, adherence might be confounded by opponent strength, injuries, etc. There is risk of lookahead if the recommended mix is derived from data that includes outcomes (e.g., using full-series data to determine which play types were effective, then testing if adherence to that retrospective mix predicts winning). That would be circular. So careful to define recommendations based only on pre-series or first-half data, etc.

The question says "suppression-conditional recommended mix". That suggests that the recommended mix is conditional on the defense's suppression strategy, which could be observed in real time or from earlier games in the series. So we could use first-half of series or previous series data to define the defense's tendencies and the engine's recommended counter-mix. Then test if adherence in the remainder of the series predicts series win. That avoids lookahead but reduces sample further because only later games? Actually series length up to 7 games, so maybe we can use first few games to learn and remaining games to test adherence. But then we need enough games per series. Could also use regular season data to define defense suppression profile and recommended mix for each team, then test if adherence in the playoff series (using that playbook) predicts series outcome. That would use all playoff games but could still be post-hoc if the regular season data is from after the fact? The data includes 2022-23 to 2025-26, so we can use prior regular season to define the defense profile, then measure adherence in the playoff series. But defense strategies may change over time (nonstationarity). Also, the defense's suppression profile may be opponent-specific.

The historical evidence shows that the engine's recommendation accuracy is questionable and prone to artifacts (SF-APPS-003 was artifact due to lookahead). SF-APPS-018 had inconclusive ranking validation with small sample and leakage. So the underlying engine may not be reliable. So testing adherence to its recommendations may not be meaningful if the recommendations themselves are not valid. That's a major risk: if the recommended mix is not actually optimal, then adherence might not correlate with winning, or could even be negatively correlated if the engine is flawed. So the question implies that the recommended mix is a good counter, which is not established. So testability is low because we need to first validate the recommendation system, or we'd be testing a joint hypothesis of adherence and recommendation quality. But the question as posed is "Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning." It does not require that the mix is optimal; just that adherence to whatever recommended mix (presumably the engine's) predicts winning. So if the engine is good, adherence may correlate; if engine is bad, adherence may not, or could be negative. So it's testable as a predictive hypothesis, but the recommendation engine's quality is a confound.

However, the historical failures with lookahead leakage and small sample suggest that many of these research questions have been plagued by artifacts. We should note that similar attempts to evaluate engine recommendations by outcomes (hit rate) resulted in artifacts (SF-APPS-003). So a design must avoid using the same data to define the recommendations and evaluate the outcome. That is a key risk: LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD. Also SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER is a risk because 54 series with binary outcome (win/loss) will require large effect size to detect.

Potential confounders: team quality, opponent strength, injuries, home-court advantage, etc. Could control with team strength metrics or use series-level matched pairs? Not easy.

So I'll now assemble the response.

First, research concepts: defensive suppression, recommended mix, adherence, winning (series win). Methodological questions: how to measure recommended mix (definition, source), how to measure adherence, how to define winning, how to avoid lookahead leakage, adequate sample size at series level, confounding.

Historical evidence: list the four records with their status as recorded (artifact, inconclusive, artifact, inconclusive). Failed approaches: SF-APPS-003: engine hit rate test artifact due to lookahead leakage and labeling flaw; SF-APPS-018: ranking validation inconclusive due to small sample, leakage, measurement reliability; SF-APPS-068: PCI artifact from mechanical floor/leakage; SF37: inconclusive due to proxy fidelity and leakage.

What evidence establishes: The engine's play-type recommendations have shown fragile signal in small-sample, potentially biased studies, with lookahead leakage being a recurrent problem. The franchise has not tested whether following the engine's recommended mix predicts series-level winning. So not answered.

What it does not establish: That adherence to recommended mix predicts winning, nor that the engine's recommendations are causally effective.

Own inferences: The question can be framed as a test of the engine's practical value if implemented, but requires careful temporal separation to avoid leakage. The small sample of 54 series makes a binary-outcome test underpowered for plausible effect sizes; a continuous outcome (e.g., net rating in series) might improve power but would still be limited.

Uncertainties: whether the recommended mix can be defined purely on data available before the game(s) in which adherence is measured; whether the defense's suppression tendencies can be reliably inferred; whether the engine's recommendations are stable across seasons.

Historical effect: changed_decision? I think the historical evidence reveals significant risks that should change the decision from a naive "proceed" to "proceed_with_changes" or "do_not_proceed". I'd say it changes the decision because without history, one might think it's a straightforward correlation, but the evidence shows lookahead artifacts have plagued similar studies, so a rigorous design is required. I'll say "yes" and explain that the evidence motivates strict temporal separation, use of independent data for recommendation generation, and awareness of power limitations.

Testability: p_testable: maybe 0.3? 54 series is low, and the recommendation engine's quality is uncertain, so the probability that a meaningful test can be done is moderate. Blocking constraints: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (54 series), LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MEASURE_RELIABILITY (defining suppression-conditional mix), CONFOUNDING.

Prior work: already_answered: no (no direct test). cited: the four families, but they didn't answer the question.

Risks: LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD (if recommendations use information from the same series or future games), SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (binary outcome with 54 series), MEASURE_RELIABILITY (suppression detection, recommended mix may be noisy), CONFOUNDING (team strength, injuries, opponent quality), DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY (defense strategies change across seasons), MULTIPLE_TESTING if multiple metrics of adherence are tried.

Predicted outcome: supported probability low due to likely null or artifact risk; rejected probability maybe moderate if null is true; untestable maybe due to design issues; artifact probability high if not careful; uncertain if inconclusive. I'll assign probabilities: supported 0.1, rejected 0.3, untestable 0.2, artifact 0.3, uncertain 0.1? Sum to 1. Actually artifact might be 0.3, untestable 0.2, rejected 0.3, supported 0.1, uncertain 0.1.

Decision: proceed_with_changes or do_not_proceed? I lean towards proceed_with_changes if a rigorous design can be specified: use only data from prior regular seasons (or first N games of series held out) to define defense suppression profiles and engine's recommended mix, then measure adherence in later games and test predictive power for series outcome, with appropriate statistical corrections for multiple comparisons. But 54 series may still be underpowered. So maybe do_not_proceed due to insufficient sample size and high risk of artifact. However, the question says "Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed." So I could recommend not to proceed, but still provide a design. I'll decide "do_not_proceed" because the combination of small sample (54 series) and high risk of lookahead artifact, plus the unproven engine, makes a convincing test unlikely. However, the design could still be described as a minimum viable test. I'll produce both.

But I think it's better to say "proceed_with_changes" with strict pre-registration, using out-of-sample recommendations and continuous outcome to boost power. But I'm not sure. Let's think: with 54 series, if we use binary outcome (series win), adherence as a predictor, maybe a logistic regression. Power analysis: suppose adherence has an R-squared of maybe 0.1 with winning, n=54, power low. Could use within-series adherence variation? Possibly use game-level adherence and predict game outcome, then aggregate? That would increase sample size (e.g., 54 series x ~5.5 games = ~297 games). So a game-level analysis with adherence per game as predictor, controlling for home/away, could be more powerful. So that's a change: unit of analysis per game, with series-level clustering. So proceed with changes: use per-game adherence to recommended mix as predictor of game outcome, with series-level random effects. That could be testable. So proceed_with_changes.

I'll design: estimand: relationship between per-game adherence to recommended offensive mix and game outcome (win/loss), conditional on defense suppression strategy derived from prior data. Unit: game. Sample: all playoff games from 2022-23 to 2025-26 with defined suppression profiles from regular season of the same season (or previous). Power: n~300 games, binary outcome, moderate effect size detectable? Could be okay. Controls: opponent defensive strength, home/away, team rankings, etc. Falsification: test that adherence to a randomly permuted recommended mix has no correlation. Multiplicity: single pre-registered adherence metric. Decision rule: if adherence coefficient positive and significant at alpha=0.05 after adjustment for multiple comparisons within series. Data version: fixed before analysis.

So decision: proceed_with_changes. The historical evidence changed the decision by highlighting the need for temporal separation to avoid lookahead, and by suggesting the use of game-level data to mitigate power issues.

Now, craft the final output with all fields.

I'll list historical evidence objects for each record with exact status as recorded: "artifact" for APPS-003, "inconclusive" for APPS-018, "artifact" for APPS-068, "inconclusive" for SF37. The findings: short summaries.

Failed approaches: For APPS-003: approach "engine top pt_shift vs team modal PT hit rate test" why "apparent effect produced by lookahead leakage and labeling flaw (artifact)". APPS-018: "ranked playsheet validation" why "inconclusive due to small sample, leakage, measurement reliability". APPS-068: "PCI incremental R2 over ORtg" why "artifact from mechanical floor, leakage tracking DRtg". SF37: "proxy engine possession-level test" why "inconclusive due to low proxy fidelity and leakage".

Now own inferences: "The recommendation engine's predictive validity is not established, so adherence to its recommendations could be testing noise. The question can be reframed as a game-level test to increase statistical power. Strict temporal separation is necessary to avoid lookahead leakage."

Uncertainties: "The stability of defense suppression profiles across regular season to playoffs may be low; the recommended mix may change with game context; measurement of adherence requires fine-grained classification of play types which may be noisy."

Historical effect: yes, changed_decision: yes, explanation: "Historical evidence of lookahead-induced artifacts in prior engine validation studies (SF-APPS-003, SF-APPS-068) and limited sample size issues (SF-APPS-018) shifted the design from a naive series-level correlation to a game-level test with temporal separation and out-of-sample recommendation generation."

Testability: p_testable: 0.35 (given moderate power with game-level analysis but risks remain). Blocking constraints: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (54 series, but game-level mitigates), LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MEASURE_RELIABILITY.

Prior work: already_answered: no. cited: [FAM:SF-APPS-003, FAM:SF-APPS-018, FAM:SF-APPS-068, FAM:SF37]. summary: "No prior study tested whether adherence to recommended mix predicts series or game outcomes; previous work focused on engine recommendation hit rates and play-type ranking, with multiple studies flagged as artifact or inconclusive."

Risks: list codes with text. Include LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, CONFOUNDING, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY.

Predicted outcome: assign probabilities as above.

Decision: proceed_with_changes.

Design: estimand: "Effect of per-game adherence to suppression-conditional recommended offensive mix on game win probability." unit: "individual playoff game". sample: "All playoff games from 2022-23 through 2025-26 for which a defense suppression profile can be estimated from the prior regular season (or earlier series games) without lookahead." power: "Approximately 300 games; logistic regression with series-level clusters; detectable effect size if adherence increases win probability by at least 5 percentage points per standard deviation increase in adherence at 80% power (simulation to be conducted)." controls: "Team offensive and defensive ratings from regular season, home/away indicator, opponent defensive strength, possibly injury report indicators." falsification: "Shuffle the recommended play-type list within each game (identity of top recommendations) and test that adherence to a random list does not predict game outcome; also test that adherence is not merely a proxy for general offensive efficiency by controlling for possession-level points." multiplicity: "Single pre-registered adherence metric: proportion of possessions using a play type in the top-3 recommended counters, weighted by possession count." decision_rule: "Positive and statistically significant coefficient (p < 0.025 in a one-sided test after Bonferroni correction if multiple metrics)." data_version: "snapshot as of 2026-06-16, using only data prior to each game (point-in-time) for recommendation generation."

That should cover it.
